Not my Recipe. It was originally posted by Reddit User Ramen-Lord some years ago. I have made it and it is tasty. it is a good guide for a beginner and you can tweak it to your taste as you gain more experience.

...I use chicken feet to boost the gelatin levels, but not by much! Just to provide some body. The stock itself won't gel quite as firmly as others recipes I've posted, and that's ok! It's suppose to have a light mouthfeel. It takes a bit of finesse t get there )making sure to barely simmer the stock at all, with as little agitation as possible), but the result is a clean and intense chicken flavor that permeates the dish, Here are the steps for each of the components you'll need:

Broth:

  • One chicken (carcass), broken down (deboned)
  • 6 chicken feet, blanched, toes and yellow membrane removed (I find 2 just fine)
  • One onion, quartered
  • 10-15 cloves of garlic, peeled
  • One two inch long piece of ginger
  • 3 carrots peeled
  • Sake
  • Mirin (rice vinegar)

Add the chicken feet, chicken parts, and vegetables, to a pot

Cover with cold water by at least an inch, and heat on high, until scum begins to rise.

Once bubbles begin to rise fairly often, back the heat down, and skim the scum that collects on the surface for the next hour or so.

Once the scum stops rising, feel free to add some sake and mirin (you can skip adding mirin here) Personal preference. (I usually add sake by smell. I add small amounts till I can detect the smell of alcohol in the broth. If you can't get sake, white cooking wine or shaoxing chinese cooking wine are fine)

Leave this alone, uncovered, and allow it to cook at the tiiiiiiinest of simmers, for at least 3 hours. I went for 10, which is probably too long. 6 is probably ideal (yep, do with 6 our simmer time. You can make broth in crockpot that had a high and low setting if you don't have a stove top).

Tare

Shio tare is the most mysterious of tare, in that it can range in texture, complexity and method. The shio tare I use is essentially a dashi of kastuo and niboshi, boiled down and heavily salted. It adds complexity I like withut being overpowering. It does cloud the stock a bit though...

There are certainly other versions of shio tare, some probably better suited fr other broth styles, but for this chicken variant, I really like this one.

  • 5 squares of konbu (3 inch x 3 inch)
  • 3/4 cup dried shitake
  • Water
  • 1 cup niboshi (dried, salted baby fishies)
  • 1/2 cup loosely packed katsuo (fish flakes) * Seasame seed oil * Mirin * Sake * Shoyu

The night before, combine several squares of kombu with a cup and a half of dried shiitake, and cover with cold water. Let this it in the fridge until ready to make tare.

In a saucepan, combine the niboshi and katsu with a tsp of seasame seed oil. Stir fry over hight heat (use non stick pan) until fragrant and the niboshi begin to brown, about 30 seconds.

Add the kombu, shiitake and water. Bring to a boil, and just before boil, remove the kombu. Simmer for 2 minutes or until dashi feels fully flavored.

Strain the solids, add the dashi back to the pot, along with a generous seasoning of salt, mirin, and sake (perhaps some soy as well). Cook this at a simmer for 10 minutes or untl reduced to a salty/intensely flavored point. This is your seasoning component, make it count!

Note about tare. If you are allergic to fish or can't find the special dried fishes you can omit those steps without harming your flavor. Instead soak your kombu and mushrooms for 2-3 days instead. You have to use a full bodied shoyu or you will get no flavor. I recommend using less or no salt and more shoyu. Shoyu/mirin ratio of about 2:1 is good flavor that most will like. Seasame seed oil does not need to be cooked into the tare and can be added by drops at serving time. When flavoring and reducing your tare, consider that 2 tables spoons of tare should be able to flavor 1 cup of broth (1 serving ramen). When serving ramen with a seperate tare, pour the tare first, then half the broth, add noodles and toppings then add rest of broth. Serving this way does make a difference
